title: Honest sweat
hookLine: in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread (Genesis 3:19)
last: OURS TO GROW, AND OURS TO GUARD.

lines: IN THE SWEAT OF THY FACE.
cards: Thorns. A field that fights back. In Genesis chapter three, after the fruit, the ground changes.

The man is told it will bring forth thorns and thistles. Then comes a line that sounds like every long shift, every harvest, every back that aches by evening: “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread.”
The garden of chapter two had a gardener. Now the gardener sweats. Today: honest sweat.

teach.h: CURSED IS THE GROUND, NOT THE JOB.
teach.b: First, read closely. In the King James text, the word cursed lands on the ground: “cursed is the ground for thy sake.” The job from chapter two isn't canceled.
What changes is the resistance: thorns, thistles, soil that won't cooperate. Some readers hear punishment here. Some hear a plain description of the world as it is, where good things take effort.
Both readings stay close to the words.
Second, sweat, then bread. The verse ties the two together: effort, and then food on the table. There's a quiet dignity in that order.
Bread in this story isn't handed down from the sky. It's earned with the body.

Third, the rest of the verse is sobering: “till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.” The worker is made of the same ground he works.
On Ash Wednesday, some Christians hear words drawn from this verse as ashes are marked on their foreheads. Fourth, sweat doesn't stay bitter everywhere in the Bible.

A psalm says of the one who walks in God's ways: “For thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands: happy shalt thou be, and it shall be well with thee.” The same hands, the same labor, and now happiness.
Put chapter three and that psalm side by side, and honest sweat looks like this: tired arms, real bread, and a day spent on something that fed someone.

how: Some Christians hear words from Genesis 3:19 on Ash Wednesday as ashes are marked on their foreheads, and Jewish and Christian readers turn to this chapter and to Psalm 128 when they speak of the dignity of hard work.

o: a fever sweat that comes from guilt or from fear
sweat from exercise done only for its own sake
real effort with the body that puts bread on the table

s: in the King James text of Genesis 3, the ground is what's cursed
“cursed is the ground for thy sake” (Genesis 3:17).
the Bible only ever treats work as punishment
Psalm 128 calls the one who eats the work of their hands happy.
Genesis 3:19 ends with dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return
the sweat verse closes by remembering what the worker is made of.

games.q: you're working a field full of thistles after Eden. reading the King James text closely, what is cursed?
games.why: “cursed is the ground for thy sake.” the tending from chapter two still stands; the ground now resists.

practice: Feel your body as a working thing, shoulders, forearms, hands, and notice what it has carried this week: groceries, a child, a box, a keyboard for too many hours.
Bring to mind one task that needs real effort and has been waiting, a floor to scrub, a hill to walk, sized to whatever your body can do today, and picture yourself starting.
If you pray, you can hold that work in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Honest sweat. From Genesis: in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread. Effort, then bread, from people made of the ground they work. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: tired arms, real bread. Effort first, and then the table. See you tomorrow.
